tagline: Canyon rock and wagon routes shape a journey through eastern Oregon
intro: The Snake River-Mormon Basin Back Country Byway crosses 150 miles of eastern Oregon rangeland in Baker and Malheur counties. Its remote roads mix pavement, gravel and earth, with steep canyons, cliffs and large rock outcrops along the way. The Bureau of Land Management presents this back country byway as a drive through rangelands, sagebrush plateaus and vegetation along waterways. Allow at least five hours behind the wheel, before stops.

Wagon roads crossed this country as ranching, mining, logging and homesteading spread through the area in the late 1800s. At Huntington, Miller's Stagecoach Station opened in 1870; two railway lines joined there in 1884, making the town a railway division point. Near the National Historic Oregon Trail Interpretive Center, protected wagon ruts preserve visible traces of the earlier journey.

From Baker City, Oregon Route 86 heads past the interpretive center toward Richland. Along Snake River Road, basalt outcrops rise above the road until it reaches Brownlee Reservoir; metamorphic and sedimentary rock then dominate toward Huntington. Rye Valley lies along Dixie Creek southeast of Baker City. Baker City sits between the Wallowa Mountains to the east and the Elkhorn Mountains to the west, with the Powder River flowing through downtown on its way to the Snake.

moments.title: Snake River Road
moments.text: The rock changes along Snake River Road. High above Brownlee Reservoir, large basalt outcrops display variations in color above the road. Once the road reaches the reservoir, metamorphic and sedimentary rock dominate the stretch toward Huntington. The wider landscape includes steep canyons, prominent cliffs, sagebrush plateaus and vegetation along waterways. In spring, wildflowers grow on the green hills.
moments.notice: Notice the color variations in basalt outcrops above Snake River Road.

moments.title: Huntington
moments.text: Huntington grew from a stagecoach stop into a railway junction. Miller's Stagecoach Station opened in 1870, and in 1884 the Oregon Short Line and Oregon Railroad and Navigation Company joined their rails here. In 1898, the Northwest Railroad Company began extending another line down the Snake River. It gave Eagle and Pine Valley fruit, cattle, lumber and ore an outlet through Huntington. Water from Brownlee Dam later flooded that line. Remnants of the older Oregon Trail remain visible along U.S. Route 30 north from Farewell Bend toward Huntington, another surviving trace of the journeys that passed through this area.

moments.title: Rye Valley
moments.text: Rye Valley takes its name from a native grass that fed the pack animals of the region's immigrants and miners in the 1860s. The settlement lies along Dixie Creek, a tributary of the Burnt River, west of Interstate 84. Its post office opened in 1869 and operated intermittently until 1935.

practical: Snake River Road: The byway has remote paved, gravel and earthen roads. BLM advises high-clearance two-wheel drive and care when planning after weather events or during winter. (checked 2026-10-11)
